cells.tense: You can hold what's in front of you without needing to pin it down.
cells.ask: Say the thing as it stands. Let one person disagree without you amending it.
cells.core:
More than one thing about a situation can sit in you at once, and you don't have to force it into a verdict. People tell you more than they meant to, because you aren't steering them toward a single answer. That much is steady and you can lean on it.

Holding a question open still takes a tolerance for the unfinished, and there's a pull to close it early just to be done. So say the thing as it stands. One person, one plain statement, and let them disagree without stepping in to soften the edges. Whether they agree isn't the point. Saying it plainly, once, is the whole of it.
cells.sheetLine: You can keep more than one truth in view without forcing a verdict.
cells.verb: holding more than one truth at once

cells.tense: You're living a step ahead of the room you're actually in.
cells.ask: Write one thing you're about to say, then wait a day before you say it.
cells.core:
You're reading people ahead of the moment — how they'll take it, which version will land, what you'll need ready when they speak. None of that has happened yet. You're dealing with forecasts instead of the person in front of you, and the conversation you've prepared isn't the one you're in. Reading what's actually there is a different move, and it mostly means stopping before the rehearsal starts.

The pressure to keep working the material into shape before anyone responds is what's putting the next moment out of reach. So write down one thing you're about to say and wait a day before you say it. Often the room has already moved on its own, or the speech turns out to have been written for a listener who didn't show.
cells.sheetLine: You're answering a reaction nobody has had yet.

cells.tense: You stopped putting weight on what you notice and started waiting for confirmation.
cells.ask: Name one thing you noticed this week before checking it against anyone else.
cells.core:
What you notice tends to come out secondhand now, if it comes out at all — held back until someone else agrees with it or says it first. When this is working, it looks like saying what you see plainly, being comfortable not knowing yet, and acting on an impression without needing the room to sign off first.

What you noticed this week is still with you, and so is the habit of keeping it until someone else confirms it. Pick one of those noticings and say it out loud as it came to you, without testing it first. Small, unfinished, yours. Say it once and see what comes back from the room.
cells.sheetLine: You notice it and wait for permission to say it.
cells.verb: holding more than one truth at once

cells.tense: You're clearing space for people and calling it just how things worked out.
cells.ask: Name one thing you set down this month and call it a choice you made.
cells.core:
You let things go — plans, conversations, people — and the story you tell yourself is that it happened on its own. It didn't. When this is clean, it looks like knowing what to keep, setting things down on purpose, and saying so without ceremony, because there's nothing to defend and nothing to explain.

The choice is still being made and the saying hasn't caught up. Pick one thing you set down recently and call it your decision. Not a confession and not a boast. Just signing something you already did, with your own name on it. That is the whole ask, and it can be done today.
cells.sheetLine: You set it down on purpose and called it how things went.
cells.verb: holding more than one truth at once

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person's read of situations 'holds up' — the record says the capacity is operating and integrated, not that it is accurate. A reader could reasonably object that they are often wrong about people and just quiet about it. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person: 'Your read holds up' — praise of a method I invented for them; cut.
